title: Build your own dynamic array
summary: Write a small std::vector from scratch: a class that owns heap memory, grows geometrically, survives being copied (the rule of three), and checks its bounds — all under AddressSanitizer.

steps.title: A class that owns memory
hints: Constructor: `IntArray::IntArray(std::size_t size) : data_(new int[size]()), size_(size) {}` — the `()` after `new int[size]` zero-fills the array.
Destructor: `delete[] data_;` — `delete[]` because it came from `new[]`.
`operator[]` returns `data_[index]`. Write it twice: once returning `int&`, once marked `const` returning `const int&`.

steps.title: Growing: size, capacity and push_back
hints: Add `std::size_t capacity_;` to the class, and make *every* constructor initialise it. Add the declarations `IntArray();`, `std::size_t capacity() const;` and `void push_back(int value);`.

push_back: if `size_ == capacity_`, allocate a bigger buffer (double it; start at, say, 4), copy the old elements across, `delete[]` the old buffer, and point `data_` at the new one. Then store the value at `data_[size_]` and `++size_`.

quiz.question: With the new copy tests, the test program fails `copies_are_independent` and AddressSanitizer reports "attempting double-free". Why?
options: `IntArray b = a;` is a compile error that the compiler missed.

The compiler-generated copy constructor copies each member — including the pointer `data_`. Now `a` and `b` share one buffer: writing `b[0]` changes `a[0]`, and both destructors `delete[]` the same memory.
push_back has a bug that only shows up when arrays are copied.
AddressSanitizer is reporting a false positive.
explanations: It compiles — that's the problem. The compiler happily writes a copy constructor for you; it just doesn't know what your pointer *means*.
Exactly. A member-by-member copy of a pointer is a **shallow copy**: two objects, one buffer, two owners. The fix is a **deep copy**: give the new object its own buffer with the same contents.
The tests that only use push_back passed. The failure starts with the first test that copies.
Sanitizers have essentially no false positives for this kind of error. When ASan says double-free, something was freed twice.

steps.title: The rule of three
hints: Declare `IntArray(const IntArray& other);` and `IntArray& operator=(const IntArray& other);` in the class.
Copy constructor: allocate a new buffer of `other.capacity_` (or nullptr if it's 0), copy `other.size_` elements, copy size_ and capacity_.

Assignment: if `this == &other` return `*this`. Otherwise make a full copy first (`IntArray copy(other);`), then `delete[]` your old buffer, take over the copy's members, and set `copy.data_ = nullptr` so the copy's destructor doesn't free them.

steps.title: Challenge: bounds checking

checks.label: Hidden acceptance tests pass
checks.failMessage: Your tests pass, but the hidden tests found a problem. Did you check every boundary — index == size, empty arrays, const arrays, popping until empty?

hints: `if (index >= size_) throw std::out_of_range("index out of range");` — `#include <stdexcept>`.
You need two `at`s, like `operator[]`: one returning `int&`, one `const` returning `const int&`.
pop_back only needs `--size_` — the memory stays allocated for the next push_back. Throw if `size_ == 0` first.
